questions.title: Why does the partition function $Z(x)$ disappear in the DPO preference model derivation?
questions.question_body:
In Section 3 the authors start from the optimal policy under a KL‐constrained objective
$$\pi_r(y\mid x)=\frac{1}{Z(x)}\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp\bigl(\tfrac{1}{\beta}r(x,y)\bigr),$$
and then re‑parameterize the reward as
$$r(x,y)=\beta \log \frac{\pi_r(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}+\beta \log Z(x).$$
When they plug this into the Bradley‑Terry model they claim that $Z(x)$ cancels out, yielding Eq.(5).
Can someone show the algebraic steps that make $Z(x)$ disappear? I'm especially confused about why the term $\log Z(x)$ vanishes after taking the difference $r^*(x,y_1)-r^*(x,y_2)$.

questions.title: What is the intuition behind the weighting term $\sigma(\hat r_{\theta}(x,y_l)-\hat r_{\theta}(x,y_w))$ in the DPO gradient?
questions.question_body:
Equation (7) gives the gradient of the DPO loss as
$$-\beta \mathbb{E}\big[ \sigma(\hat r_{\theta}(x,y_l)-\hat r_{\theta}(x,y_w)) ( \nabla_{{\theta}} \log \pi_{\theta}(y_w|x) - \nabla_{\theta}\log \pi_{\theta}(y_l|x) ) \big].$$
Why do we multiply the log‑probability updates by the sigmoid of the reward difference? How does this weighting prevent model degeneration compared to a naïve "unlikelihood" loss where we would simply increase $y_w$ and decrease $y_l$ without any weight?

questions.title: How does the hyper‑parameter $\beta$ control the trade‑off between reward maximisation and KL‑regularisation in DPO?
questions.question_body:
Both Eq.(3) and Eq.(6) contain a factor $\beta$ that appears inside a log‑ratio and also multiplies the whole loss (through the sigmoid argument). I understand that $\beta$ has a similar role to the KL penalty coefficient in RLHF, but I’m not clear on its concrete effect:

* If I increase $\beta$, do I make the policy stay closer to the reference model or push it more aggressively towards high‑reward responses?
* Is there an intuitive way to choose $\beta$, e.g., based on desired KL budget?
* How does changing $\beta$ affect gradient magnitudes during training?

questions.title: Why are two reward functions that differ by a function of $x$ considered equivalent under Bradley‑Terry?
questions.question_body:
Definition 1 says that $r(x,y)$ and $r'(x,y)$ are equivalent iff there exists an $f(x)$ such that $r(x,y)-r'(x,y)=f(x)$. Lemma 1 then claims that such equivalent rewards induce identical preference distributions.
Can someone give a concrete example illustrating this equivalence, and explain why adding an $x$‑only offset does not change pairwise preference probabilities?

questions.title: What assumptions are required for Theorem 1 (the reparameterisation theorem) to hold?
questions.question_body:
Theorem 1 states that every reward class compatible with Bradley‑Terry/Plackett‑Luce can be represented as
$$r(x,y)=\beta \log \frac{\pi(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}$$
for some policy $\pi$. The proof mentions "mild assumptions" but does not enumerate them.
* Does it require that both $\pi$ and $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ have full support over possible completions?
* Are there smoothness or boundedness conditions on the reward function?
* How critical is the choice of reference policy for this equivalence?
Any clarification would help me understand when DPO’s reparameterisation may fail.

questions.title: How is the reference policy $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ constructed when no SFT model is available?
questions.question_body: In Section 3, when a supervised fine‑tuned model is not provided, authors propose to obtain $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ by maximizing likelihood on preferred completions $(x,y_w)$. Why is fitting only on preferred answers sufficient to approximate a good reference distribution? Wouldn't this bias $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ towards high‑reward regions and reduce diversity? Are there alternative strategies for building $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ from preference data alone?

questions.title: Why does DPO outperform PPO even when PPO has access to ground‑truth rewards (PPO‑GT)?
questions.question_body:
In Figure 2 (sentiment experiment), DPO dominates PPO‑GT on both reward and KL axes despite PPO‑GT using the true sentiment classifier as reward.
* Is this purely due to variance reduction from avoiding sampling in PPO?
* Does DPO benefit from an exact analytic gradient whereas PPO relies on REINFORCE style estimates?
* Could any hyper‑parameter tuning (e.g., learning rates, baselines) close this gap for PPO?
I’d like to understand which part of PPO’s pipeline causes its inefficiency relative to DPO.

questions.title: How does Direct Preference Optimization relate to control‑as‑inference frameworks?
questions.question_body:
Section 4 derives an actor–critic objective (Eq.~9) that resembles a control‑as‑inference formulation where we minimize KL$(π_θ||π^*)$. In standard control‑as‑inference, a "soft value" term appears as an expectation over future rewards.
* In DPO, why does rewriting the reward eliminate the need for an explicit baseline/value function?
* Does DPO implicitly treat the KL term as part of a logarithmic normaliser, thus performing exact inference without approximation?
I’m trying to map each term in Eq.~9 onto its counterpart in typical control‑as‑inference literature.

questions.title: Can DPO be extended beyond binary preferences to multi‑ranking or listwise preferences?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions extensions to Plackett–Luce models in Appendix C but focuses on Bradley–Terry (pairwise) data. If I have human annotations that rank three or more completions per prompt, how would the loss change? Would we still use a binary cross entropy over log‑ratio terms, or is there a natural listwise loss derived from Eq.(5)?

questions.title: What practical considerations arise when computing log‑probability ratios across long generated sequences?
questions.question_body:
The DPO loss requires evaluating $
abla_θ \log \pi_θ(y|x)$ for both preferred and dispreferred completions, which involves summing token log probabilities over potentially long texts.
* Do we need to recompute full sequence probabilities at each update step, or can we cache token‐level logits?
* How does teacher forcing affect gradient stability when training on generated samples rather than ground truth tokens?
* Are there numerical issues (e.g., underflow) when taking ratios of very small probabilities?
Any implementation tips would be appreciated.

questions.title: Why do different GPT‑4 prompts yield different win rates when evaluating DPO models?
questions.question_body: Section 5 reports that using a "concise" prompt versus a "simple" prompt changes GPT‑4’s win rates relative to human judgments. Is this variation due solely to prompt wording affecting GPT‑4’s bias toward length, or does it indicate deeper reliability concerns when using LLMs as evaluators? How should one choose or calibrate evaluation prompts for future work on preference optimisation?

questions.title: How would Direct Preference Optimization handle multi‑turn dialogue where preferences depend on earlier turns?
questions.question_body: The current formulation assumes a single prompt–response pair $(x,y)$ with preferences over two completions. In multi‑turn settings, human feedback may evaluate entire conversation histories. Can DPO be applied by treating each turn as an independent preference pair, or is there a principled way to incorporate context‐dependent preferences into Eq.(6)? What modifications would be required in theory and implementation?
